hints: Look at what controls the resistance of a metal wire - its length, its thickness and the material it is made from. Check your length is in SI base units before you calculate.
Link resistivity $\rho$, length $L$ and cross-sectional area $A$ with $$R = \frac{\rho L}{A}$$ and convert $150\text{ cm}$ to $1.5\text{ m}$.
Substitute $\rho = 1.12 \times 10^{-6}\text{ }\Omega\text{ m}$, $L = 1.5\text{ m}$ and $A = 2.45 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m}^2$, then round to three significant figures with unit $\Omega$.
walkthrough:
**Picture What Resistivity Means**
Think of resistivity $\rho$ as how strongly the material itself opposes current. A longer wire gives more opposition, a fatter wire gives less. That is why resistance grows with length $L$ and shrinks with area $A$.

**Get Units Ready**
You are given $L = 150\text{ cm}$, $A = 2.45 \times 10^{-7}\text{ m}^2$ and $\rho = 1.12 \times 10^{-6}\text{ }\Omega\text{ m}$. Convert length to metres: $$L = 150\text{ cm} = 1.50\text{ m}$$ Area and resistivity are already in SI units, so you can substitute directly.

**Calculate Resistance**
Use: $$R = \frac{\rho L}{A}$$ $$R = \frac{(1.12 \times 10^{-6}) \times 1.5}{2.45 \times 10^{-7}}$$ $$R = 6.857...\text{ }\Omega \approx 6.86\text{ }\Omega$$ Keep three significant figures as requested.
Final answer: $R = 6.86\text{ }\Omega$ to three significant figures.

hints: Focus on the word null - it means zero. Think about what instrument is adjusted until it shows zero and why that means no current flows in that branch.
walkthrough:
**Why Zero Matters**
In Fig. 7.1 the sliding contact is moved until the galvanometer shows no deflection. At that point the p.d. across that length of nichrome wire exactly balances the e.m.f. of cell X, so no current flows through cell X and the galvanometer. That balance position is the null point.
Final answer: A null method is one where the galvanometer reading is adjusted to zero, so no current flows in the test circuit.

hints: Remember the nichrome wire is uniform, so the p.d. across any part of it is proportional to its length. At the null point, the e.m.f. of cell X equals the p.d. across 64 cm of the wire.
Set up the length ratio for the 150 cm wire driven by 1.2 V: e.m.f. of X divided by 1.2 V equals 64 cm divided by 150 cm, then solve for the e.m.f.
walkthrough:
**Use Uniform Potential Gradient**
Because the wire is uniform and carries a steady current, voltage drops evenly along it. The full $1.2\text{ V}$ is across the full $150\text{ cm}$.

**Apply the Balance Condition**
At null, e.m.f. of X = p.d. across balance length: $$\frac{E_X}{1.2} = \frac{64}{150}$$ $$E_X = \frac{64}{150} \times 1.2$$ $$E_X = 0.512\text{ V} \approx 0.51\text{ V}$$

hints: Think about what happens inside the new driver cell when current flows through it - some of its 1.2 V e.m.f. is used up inside the cell itself.
If less p.d. is left across the nichrome wire, the voltage per cm falls. Decide whether you now need more or less wire length to still balance the same cell X.
walkthrough:
**Lost Volts Reduces Wire p.d.**
With internal resistance $r$, the driver current causes a drop $Ir$ inside the cell. The terminal p.d. across the wire is: $$V = E - Ir$$ So $V$ across the 150 cm wire is now less than $1.2\text{ V}$.

**Balance Length Must Increase**
Voltage per cm along the wire is now smaller. To still get $0.51\text{ V}$ to balance the unchanged cell X, you need a greater length of wire. So the sliding contact must be moved further from the left-hand end, i.e. the null point moves to the right.

Final answer: Internal resistance causes lost volts so the p.d. across the wire (terminal p.d.) is less than 1.2 V. The p.d. per unit length falls, so a longer length is needed to balance cell X and the null point moves to the right.
